title: Child protection for teachers in Vietnam: the rules
description: Consent rules for student photos, why private lessons put your work permit at risk, the ban on harsh discipline and how to report a concern, as of 2026.
h1: Safeguarding and professional conduct for English teachers in Vietnam
intro: For a foreign English teacher in Vietnam, child protection comes from a few laws plus your employer's own policies. The Law on Teachers (in force since 1 January 2026) bans discriminating among learners and forcing them into paid extra classes, Circular 19/2025 bans violent or humiliating discipline in schools, and the personal data law needs consent from a parent and any child aged 7 or over before a child's private information is published. Keep photos, messages and paid lessons inside your employer's rules.
keyPoints: No student photo or video should leave the classroom without written consent: under Law 91/2025/QH15, publishing a child's private information needs the agreement of the parent **and** of the child if they are 7 or older, and it must stop if consent is withdrawn.
Never post students on your personal social media, and keep parent contact on the school's official Zalo groups or channels, not your private account.

Paid private lessons are the legal trap: a school teacher may not tutor their own assigned students for pay in curriculum subjects (Circular 29/2024), and a foreigner teaching privately for cash is working without a permit, fined {{vnd:15000000-25000000}} with possible deportation.
In schools, violent or humiliating discipline is banned (Circular 19/2025); primary pupils can only be reminded and asked to apologise.

Ask on day one for the work rules, the photo and communication policy, and the name of the person you report a concern to. You can only be disciplined for conduct set out in the work rules, your contract or the law.

sections.title: What Vietnamese law expects of teachers

blocks.text: Most of what governs your conduct around children comes from education rules written for Vietnamese schools, a 2025 data-protection law and the Labour Code. None of them is a safeguarding code written specifically for foreign teachers, so your employer's own policy fills most of the gaps. The table below lists the rules that most directly shape a teacher's day, as of October 2026.

blocks.caption: Rules that shape a teacher's conduct with children in Vietnam (as of October 2026; sources linked in the text below)
rows: Law on Teachers 73/2025/QH15, Art. 11(2) (in force 1 January 2026)
Teachers may not discriminate among learners, falsify assessment or admission results, force learners into extra classes, force payments beyond legal fees, or abuse their status to break the law
No favouritism, honest marks and reports, and no pushing students or parents towards paid lessons
Circular 19/2025/TT-BGDĐT (in force 31 October 2025)
Violent or humiliating discipline is prohibited; primary pupils can only be reminded and asked to apologise; secondary students can be reminded, criticised or asked to write a self-criticism
No shouting down, shaming, physical punishment or rough handling; behaviour problems go to the school
Law on Personal Data Protection 91/2025/QH15, Art. 24 (in force 1 January 2026)
Publishing or disclosing private information about a child aged 7 or over needs the consent of the child and the parent or legal representative; processing stops if consent is withdrawn
Written consent before any photo, video or personal detail of a student is shared beyond the class
Circular 29/2024/TT-BGDĐT (in force 14 February 2025), amended by Circular 19/2026 (from 15 May 2026)

A teacher at a school may not give paid out-of-school tutoring to students they are assigned to teach; tutoring must be voluntary. Since 15 May 2026, language enrichment outside the Ministry's subject programmes no longer counts as tutoring under these rules
Say no when a parent asks you to tutor their child privately; the work-permit rule below applies either way
Decree 219/2025/ND-CP and Decree 283/2026/ND-CP
A work permit covers one employer and the work it names; working without a valid permit is fined and may lead to deportation
Teach only where your permit says, and no trial, demo or cover classes before it is issued

blocks.text: The [Law on Teachers](https://xaydungchinhsach.chinhphu.vn/toan-van-luat-nha-giao-119250703171419548.htm) applies to teachers recruited to teach in institutions of the national education system, and teachers at non-public schools have their rights and pay governed by labour law ([Art. 2(1), 8(1) and 23(2)](https://hoatieu.vn/phap-luat/luat-nha-giao-217012)). The law does not say whether every provision reaches a foreign teacher at a private language centre, and we found no Government decree on recruiting foreign teachers as of October 2026. Treat its list of [things a teacher must not do](https://luatvietnam.vn/tin-van-ban-moi/quy-dinh-nhung-viec-nha-giao-khong-duoc-lam-theo-luat-nha-giao-2025-186-102922-article.html) as the standard wherever you teach: it is what parents, managers and inspectors expect.

[Circular 19/2025](https://luatvietnam.vn/tin-van-ban-moi/tu-31-10-2025-khong-con-hinh-thuc-ky-luat-dinh-chi-hoc-doi-voi-hoc-sinh-186-104157-article.html) replaced the 1988 student-discipline rules, removed suspension and expulsion, and added counselling, encouragement and monitoring as support measures. It is written for schools, but expect the same standard at a centre: any physical punishment or rough handling of a child is illegal and will end your job.

The closest thing to a background check in the system is the criminal record in your work-permit file: under Decree 219/2025 it must be issued, by your home country or by Vietnam, **no more than 6 months before the employer files** ([Decree 219/2025, Art. 18](https://congbaocdn.chinhphu.vn/CongBaoCP/VanBan/2025/8/45798/58141-1-20251073-1074219-2025-nd-cp.pdf)). The [criminal record check guide](/teach-in-vietnam/criminal-record-check-for-a-vietnam-work-permit) covers how to get it. Vietnam's wider child-protection and criminal law also applies to everyone in the country; this guide covers only the classroom-level rules above, and your employer or a lawyer has the final word on anything beyond them.

sections.title: School policies to expect, and what to ask for

blocks.text: Written policies vary a lot between an international school, a chain centre and a small kindergarten, so ask for them before you start rather than learning them from a complaint. Two Labour Code rules make this worth doing. An employer may not discipline you for conduct that is not set out in its work rules, your contract or the law ([Art. 127(3)](https://hethongphapluat.com/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019/chuong-8)). And an employer with 10 or more staff must have written work rules, which must cover preventing sexual harassment at work and the procedure for handling it ([Art. 118](https://hethongphapluat.com/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019/chuong-8)).

blocks.caption: Policies to ask for in your first week (what they cover varies by employer; get them in writing)
rows: Work rules or staff handbook
What counts as misconduct, how complaints about a teacher are handled, and what the disciplinary steps are
Photo, video and social media
Who may film students, on whose device, where files are stored, whether written parental consent is on file, and whether the centre will use your own image in advertising
Communication with parents
Which Zalo groups or apps are official, whether you post in them at all, and who answers parents' complaints
Concerns about a child
Who you report to, in what form, and how quickly
Private tutoring and contact outside class
Whether you may see students outside class, and the rules on private lessons and gifts
Cameras and observations
Whether classrooms have cameras managers can watch, and the observation rubric or KPIs used
Dress and conduct
Dress code or uniform, rules on visible tattoos, and lateness rules

blocks.text: Many teachers report that centres run scheduled and unannounced observations, that some classrooms have cameras academic managers can watch, and that parent feedback is passed straight on to the teacher. In kids' centres a Vietnamese teaching assistant is usually in the room, and in some centres the TA is also expected to film the children for parents. Agree with your TA when filming happens so the class is never left without an adult's attention.

Dress neatly and conservatively: a collared shirt or blouse, long trousers or a knee-length skirt, closed shoes. Many centres have written dress rules, and in public schools visible tattoos are best covered. Teachers who have worked or interviewed at a school can review it on eno.vn's [school directory](/schools), though most schools have few or no reviews yet. The [language centre guide](/teach-in-vietnam/language-centre-jobs-in-ho-chi-minh-city) and the [international school guide](/teach-in-vietnam/international-school-jobs-in-vietnam) cover how the two kinds of employer differ.

sections.title: Can I take photos of my students or post them online?

blocks.text: Only inside your employer's photo policy, and never on your personal accounts. Under [Article 24 of the Law on Personal Data Protection](https://hethongphapluat.com/luat-bao-ve-du-lieu-ca-nhan-2025/dieu-24) (Law 91/2025/QH15, in force 1 January 2026), processing a child's personal data to publish or disclose information about their private life needs the consent of the child, if they are 7 or older, and of the parent or legal representative ([Lawyers' Journal](https://lsvn.vn/cong-bo-du-lieu-ca-nhan-cua-tre-tu-07-tuoi-phai-duoc-nguoi-dai-dien-dong-y-a167752.html)). Processing must stop when that consent is withdrawn.

Whether a class photo sent to parents or used in an advert counts as private information is a matter of interpretation; no ruling on it was found. The safe reading is to treat every identifiable image of a student as needing written consent, from the parent and from the child if they are 7 or older.

blocks.title: The mistake that ends jobs
blocks.text: Posting a cute classroom video on your own Instagram, TikTok or Facebook, or sending it to friends, is the quickest way for a foreign teacher to break both the employer's policy and the consent rule. Keep student images on school devices or the school's own channels, and only where consent is on file.

items: Use the school's device or account for any filming the school asks for, and delete copies from your own phone.
Before any image leaves the classroom, check that written consent is on file for every child in it; ask the coordinator if you are unsure.
Leave out names, school uniforms with the school name, report cards and anything that locates a child when sharing class work.
If a parent or child asks for an image to be removed, pass it on to the school the same day: the law requires processing to stop when consent is withdrawn.

Your own image counts too: in September 2025 Ho Chi Minh City's Department of Education said some centres had used foreign teachers' photos in advertising without approval ([Tuoi Tre News](https://news.tuoitre.vn/ho-chi-minh-city-warns-language-centers-over-teacher-quality-especially-foreign-hires-103250925172100232.htm)). Agree in writing whether and how the centre may use yours.

sections.title: Contact with students and parents outside class

blocks.text: Messaging parents and students

Zalo is Vietnam's main messaging app, and homeroom teachers in Ho Chi Minh City commonly run official class groups with parents; some parents receive hundreds of group messages a day, and group disputes can escalate into attacks on teachers ([SGGP](https://www.sggp.org.vn/nhom-tro-chuyen-tren-mang-phien-phuc-cho-ca-phu-huynh-lan-hoc-sinh-post713190.html)). The city's Department of Education has urged schools to set codes of conduct for these groups.

items: Use a separate work profile, and only the groups the school names as official.
Keep messages brief, polite and about learning; raise problems privately with your coordinator rather than in the group.
Do not answer a complaint about you, or about another child, in a group chat. Pass it to the school.
Do not accept friend or follow requests from students on your personal accounts, and do not start one-to-one private chats with a child outside the school's channels.
Keep a copy of any message from a parent or student that worries you; you may need it when you report.

blocks.text: Private lessons: the rule most teachers get wrong

Parents often ask a foreign teacher to tutor their child at home. Two separate rules say no. [Circular 29/2024](https://luatvietnam.vn/tin-van-ban-moi/da-co-thong-tu-29-2024-tt-bgddt-quy-dinh-ve-day-them-hoc-them-tu-14-02-2025-186-100582-article.html), in force since 14 February 2025, bars a teacher who teaches at a school from giving paid out-of-school classes, online included, to the students they are assigned to teach, and it allows no extra classes for primary pupils except arts, sports and life skills. [Circular 19/2026](https://luatvietnam.vn/tin-van-ban-moi/da-co-thong-tu-19-2026-tt-bgddt-sua-thong-tu-29-2024-tt-bgddt-ve-day-them-hoc-them-186-108257-article.html) took foreign-language enrichment outside the Ministry's subject programmes out of these rules from 15 May 2026, so the first rule mainly bites when private lessons re-teach the school's English programme. The second rule applies either way.

The second rule is the work permit. Paid tutoring providers must be registered businesses, household-business registration is reserved for Vietnamese citizens ([Decree 168/2025, Art. 82](https://hethongphapluat.com/nghi-dinh-168-2025-nd-cp-ve-dang-ky-doanh-nghiep/dieu-82)), and your permit covers only your named employer. No regulation names foreign private tutors, but the effect is that private lessons for cash are work without a permit: under Decree 283/2026, in force since 10 September 2026, the worker is fined **{{vnd:15000000-25000000}} and may be deported** ([Suc Khoe & Doi Song](https://suckhoedoisong.vn/tu-10-9-2026-lao-dong-nuoc-ngoai-se-bi-phat-neu-khong-co-giay-phep-lao-dong-169260824224738.htm)). If you want more hours, take them as an employee of a centre that holds your permit; the [private tutoring and online teaching guide](/teach-in-vietnam/private-tutoring-and-online-teaching-in-vietnam) covers the options.

The same applies to where you teach. In an April 2026 case in Thanh Hoa, foreign teachers were found teaching at private kindergartens while their work permits named a different language centre, and officials said bringing in foreigners without permits to teach, substitute, give trial lessons or observe classes is illegal ([Bao Thanh Hoa](https://baothanhhoa.vn/vi-pham-trong-su-dung-giao-vien-nuoc-ngoai-tai-co-so-mam-non-283585.htm)). The [work permit guide](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnam-work-permit-for-english-teachers) explains what yours covers.

sections.title: Discipline, praise and conduct in the classroom

blocks.text: Vietnamese students often stay quiet and wait to be called on, and studies of Vietnamese learning culture describe face-saving as extremely important to students and their families ([Pham Thi My Hanh, NUS](https://fass.nus.edu.sg/cls/wp-content/uploads/sites/32/2020/10/pham_thimyhanh.pdf)). Sarcasm, public reprimands and shaming cause loss of face, produce parent complaints and, in schools, can cross into the humiliating discipline Circular 19/2025 bans.

items: Praise in public; correct in private or through whole-class feedback.
Use the school's reward and behaviour system rather than inventing punishments; persistent problems go to the TA, the homeroom teacher or the academic team.
Never touch a child to punish, restrain or move them roughly. Follow your school's rules on physical contact with young learners, and keep your TA or another adult in the room.
Make report-card and progress comments specific, start with something positive and give one clear next step. They are often translated and sent to parents, so avoid idioms and sarcasm.
Arrive 15 to 20 minutes early to set up and brief your TA, including when Vietnamese is acceptable (under-6s, safety, behaviour).

blocks.text: The [classroom culture guide](/teach-in-vietnam/vietnamese-classroom-culture-for-english-teachers) and the [young learners guide](/teach-in-vietnam/teaching-young-learners-in-vietnam) go further into managing quiet classes and kindergarten groups.

sections.title: How to report a concern about a child

blocks.text: We found no published reporting procedure written for foreign teachers in Ho Chi Minh City as of October 2026, so your employer's procedure is your first route. Where the school has none, the steps below follow common safeguarding practice in international schools.

items.title: If a child is in immediate danger, call for help
items.text: Call 113 for the police or 115 for an ambulance; calls are free ([VOV](https://vov.vn/xa-hoi/tphcm-ra-mat-he-thong-tong-dai-khan-cap-lien-thong-113-114-115-782233.vov)). English support is limited, so ask your TA or a Vietnamese colleague to make or join the call.

items.title: Listen, but do not investigate
items.text: If a child tells you something, let them speak, do not ask leading questions, and do not promise to keep it secret: you will have to pass it on. Do not contact the parents or the person concerned yourself.

items.title: Write down what you saw or heard
items.text: Record the date, time, place, the child's exact words and what you observed, as facts rather than opinions. Keep any messages. Store notes where other people cannot read them.

items.title: Report the same day to the person named in your policy
items.text: That is typically an academic manager, the head of centre or a named child-protection lead. Report in writing, by email or the school's system, so there is a dated record.

items.title: Follow up, and keep it confidential
items.text: Ask what happens next. Do not discuss the case with other parents, in Zalo groups or on social media. If you believe the school has not acted and a child is at risk, go to the police.

sections.title: Protecting yourself: complaints, accusations and harassment

blocks.text: Good conduct protects you as well as the children. Common safeguarding practice is to avoid being alone with one child out of sight of other adults, keep classroom doors or windows uncovered where the school allows, keep all contact on official channels, and keep a written record. If a complaint is made about you, ask for it in writing, answer through the school, and do not contact the family yourself.

Your employer cannot fine you or cut your pay as a disciplinary measure ([Labour Code Art. 127(2)](https://hethongphapluat.com/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019/chuong-8)), and dismissal as a disciplinary penalty is allowed only on the grounds listed in [Art. 125](https://hethongphapluat.com/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019/dieu-125). Sexual harassment at work, as defined in the work rules, is one of those grounds. If you are the one harassed, the law is on your side too: workplace sexual harassment that is not a crime is fined {{vnd:15000000-30000000}} under Decree 283/2026 ([VnExpress](https://vnexpress.net/phat-den-25-trieu-dong-voi-doanh-nghiep-giu-giay-to-cua-nguoi-lao-dong-5103298.html)), and you may resign without notice under Art. 35 of the [Labour Code](https://dulieuphapluat.vn/van-ban/lao-dong/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019-45716.html).

If you are dismissed and think it was unlawful, a dismissal dispute can go straight to court without mediation; you have 1 year from discovering the violation to sue, and 6 months if you want mediation first ([Labour Code, Chapter 14](https://hethongphapluat.com/bo-luat-lao-dong-2019/chuong-14)). Your embassy will not intervene with an employer, but the [UK](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/living-in-vietnam) and other governments publish lists of English-speaking lawyers. Your contract terms are covered in the [contracts guide](/teach-in-vietnam/english-teaching-contracts-in-vietnam).

faqs.q: Can I accept gifts from students and parents on Teachers' Day?
faqs.a: 20 November is Vietnamese Teachers' Day, now written into the Law on Teachers, and flowers, cards and small gifts are normal, as are red envelopes at Tet. Accept small tokens graciously and follow your employer's policy on cash or expensive gifts.

faqs.q: Will my school check my criminal record?
faqs.a: Your work-permit file must include a criminal record issued by your home country or Vietnam no more than 6 months before the employer files. If an employer asks for any further check, ask exactly what it needs before you travel.

faqs.q: Can my school fine me for breaking a conduct rule?
faqs.a: No. The Labour Code bans fines and wage cuts as discipline, and you can only be disciplined for conduct set out in the work rules, your contract or the law. Deductions are allowed only to compensate damage to the employer's property, capped at 30% of monthly pay.

faqs.q: A parent is complaining about me in the class Zalo group. Should I reply?
faqs.a: No. Do not answer in the group. Screenshot the messages, pass them to your coordinator or the academic manager, and let the school respond to the parent.

faqs.q: Can I meet a student outside school, for example for coffee or a class trip?
faqs.a: Only as part of an activity your employer organises and approves, with other adults present. Meeting a child privately, or arranging paid lessons, puts both the child and your work permit at risk.
